extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society; natural philosophers; experimental scientists and technical readers
extracted.subtask_description: Writing short experimental reports and book/experiment accounts for a learned scientific journal (Philosophical Transactions), including apparatus description, procedures, observations, and evaluations. Emphasis on clear procedural detail so other practitioners can reproduce or judge the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projection apparatus setup (image on a wall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposite to the place or wall where the apparition is to be, let a hole be made of about a foot in diameter or larger; without this hole place the picture or object inverted, and by means of looking-glasses set behind, if the picture be transparent, reflect the rays of the sun so as that they may pass through it towards the place where it is to be represented; and let the picture be encompassed on every side with a board or cloth, that no rays may pass beside it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place object inverted behind a hole; use looking-glasses to reflect sun-rays through the object to the wall; surround object with board/cloth to block stray rays. Use a broad convex-glass between object and wall so it may represent the object distinct. The nearer the convex-glass is to the object, the more magnified the image; farther off yields smaller image. If object cannot be inverted, use two large glasses placed at distances found by trials to make representations erect. All reflecting/refracting glasses and persons employed must be placed without the window or hole to avoid detection by spectators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of light sources for optical demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatsoever may be done by means of the sun-beams in the day time, the same may be done with much more ease in the night, by the help of torches, lamps, or other strong lights placed about the objects, according to the several sorts of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Daytime demonstrations: use sun-beams and reflect/refract them appropriately. Night demonstrations: use strong artificial lights (torches, lamps) arranged around the object. Choose light strength and placement according to the object (transparent picture, statue, living creature, candle, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concealment of apparatus and operators
rubrics_metrics.description: These objects, reflecting and refracting glasses, and the whole apparatus, as also the persons employed to manage them, must be placed without the window or hole, so that they may not be perceived by the spectators in the room.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apparatus and operators must be hidden from audience view to preserve effect and avoid detection; arrange all optical components outside the spectators' room and conceal by architecture or coverings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image orientation correction when object cannot be inverted
rubrics_metrics.description: If the object cannot be inverted, as it is pretty difficult to do with living animals, candles, &c., then let two large glasses of convenient spheres be placed at proper distances, to be found by trials, to make the representations erect, as well as the object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a two-lens arrangement (two large spherical glasses) with spacing determined experimentally to produce an erect image when inversion of the object is impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optical element placement controls magnification
rubrics_metrics.description: The nearer [the convex-glass] it is placed to the object, the more is the object magnified on the wall; and the farther off the less; which diversity is effected by glasses of several spheres.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Magnification of the projected image is controlled by the distance between convex-glass and object and by the lens curvature (sphere). Vary sphere/placement to tune image size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method for producing opal-like colour in glass (heat control)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is very lively, and, as I guess, performed only by the degrees of heat producing the colours. When the composition is thoroughly melted, they take out some on the point of an iron-rod, which being cooled, either in the air or water, is colourless and pellucid; but being put into the mouth of the furnace on the same rod, and there turned by the hand for a little time, its little particles take such various positions, that the light falling on them being variously modified, represents those several colours that are seen in the true opal. It is remarkable that the colours of it may be destroyed and restored again by different degrees of heat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Colour arises from controlled heating and cooling cycles that alter particle positions. Procedure: melt composition thoroughly, take a sample on an iron rod and cool (colourless), then reheat/rotate in furnace to create particle arrangements that scatter light into opal colours. Colours can be altered or restored by varying heat — practice and heat control are essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporting experimental interventions: specify substances used
rubrics_metrics.description: The public should have been told what the medicines employed in these experiments were.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting medical/therapeutic experiments (e.g., infusing medicines into veins), explicitly state the substances and dosages used so readers can assess, reproduce, and judge the experiment. Omission of what medicines were used is a substantive reporting failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful reporting of outcomes and failures
rubrics_metrics.description: Mons. Smith ... tried the opening of a vein, and infusing some medicines into the blood. This was tried upon two persons, one of whom recovered, and the other died. ... the said physician ... repeated the experiment ... three persons ... the gouty man found himself pretty well next day, ... the apoplectic patient has not had one paroxysm since ... the several sores ... are healed ... both these persons have been able to work ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both successes and failures plainly, giving patient outcomes for each trial. Note variability of outcomes, allow readers to weigh evidence rather than presenting only positive results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Device user-comfort and adjustability (empty tubes/spectacles)
rubrics_metrics.description: I have now tried convex spectacles ... and putting these glasses into the tapers, I found the smallest prints somewhat larger, but not so clear, so distinct, nor so pleasing to the eye, as when I use the empty tapers. ... I find myself best at ease with those leathern tubes I first used, and rather without any fastening to the bone of the spectacles: For, as they hang in that slight manner, I can now with a touch of my finger raise them up or bow them down, divide them or unite to take in the same object. And I put them off and on as speedily and as easily as any other spectacles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When describing or designing optical aids, report effects on clarity and ease of use and prefer adjustable, easy-to-manipulate fittings. Note comparative performance (convex spectacles vs empty tubes) and user comfort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide ocular demonstration or direct evidence for anatomical claims
rubrics_metrics.description: He affirms he can prove by ocular demonstration that the substance of the testicles is a congeries of very small vessels ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anatomical claims should be supported by direct/ocular demonstration (dissection, clear figures) and should confront contrary reports; claimants should show demonstrations or observations so that the community can verify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual completeness when publishing letters or controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: This letter is omitted, as of no satisfactory use to any person, without the animadversions which occasioned it, and which were printed in another country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When publishing a reply or part of a controversy, include the original animadversions/criticisms or sufficient context so the reply is meaningful to readers; publishing fragments without context renders them of little use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluative standards for mathematical exposition: perspicuity, ingenuity, elegance
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine on which [the book] is founded, ... is perspicuous, and ingeniously treated. The quadrature of the hyperbola ... is very elegant and ingenious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess mathematical works for clarity (perspicuity), cleverness/ingenuity of method, and elegance of presentation and proofs. These are presented as virtues in evaluating mathematical treatises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detailed observational indicators for mining prospects
rubrics_metrics.description: Experienced miners ... that the veins sometimes run up into the roots of trees, yet they observed no difference at the top. ... White, yellow, and mixed earth are leaders to the country, as they call it: changeable colours always encourage their hopes. A black stone is of bad import, as it leads to a jam, a black thick stone that hinders their work. A grey clear dry one they account best. The nearness they guess by short brittle clay; for the tough is not leading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporting mining observations, list the field indicators used by practitioners (soil colours, stone types, behaviour of snow/frost, presence of certain 'crootes', etc.) so readers understand how prospecting decisions are made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mining practice procedures and tool specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: The groove is 4 feet long, 2 1/2 feet broad, till they meet a stone, when they carry it as they can. The groove is supported by timber ... A piece of an arm's thickness will support 10 ton of earth. For the supply of fresh air there are boxes of elm exactly closed, of about six inches in the clear, by which they carry it down above 20 fathoms. ... They make use of leathern bags, eight or nine gallons a-piece, drawn up by ropes to draw up the water. ... Their ladders are of ropes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete dimensions, materials, and configurations (groove size, timber supports, air-box dimensions, leather bags capacity, hearth dimensions) for practical reproducibility. Describe tools and their expected lifetimes and constraints (e.g., axes break quickly unless hardened).

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and environmental hazard reporting in industrial operations
rubrics_metrics.description: If they cannot cut the rock, they use fire to anneal it, laying on wood and coal, and the fire is so contrived that they leave the mine before the operation begins, and find it dangerous to enter again, before it be quite cleared of the smoke, which has killed some. ... There is a flight in the smoke, which falling upon the grass, poisons the cattle that eat of it. ... If this flight mix with the water in which the ore is washed, and be carried away in a stream, it poisons cattle ... even after a course of three miles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report known hazards and precautions (evacuate before firing, wait until smoke clears). Note environmental impacts (toxic smoke/fallout contaminating grass and water, poisoning animals) and how far effects may spread; include these observations in operational accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Smelting and ore preparation procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: They beat the ore with a flat iron; then cleanse it in water from the dirt; and sift it through a wire sieve. ... For this purpose they have a hearth about five feet high, set upon timber to be turned as a windmill, to avoid the inconvenience of smoke upon a shifting wind. The hearth contains half a bushel of ore and coal, with bellows on the top. The charcoal is put upon the hearth, where the ore is; laying dry sticks upon the top, which they call their white coals. There is a sink on the side of the hearth, into which the lead runs, that holds about a hundred and a half. Then it is cast into sand, forming what are called sowes. Once melting is enough: and the best, which is heaviest, melts first.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describe ore preparation (beating, washing, sieving), hearth construction and operation (height, fuel, bellows, sink dimensions), melting and casting steps (cast into sand to form ingots), and note that best/heaviest ore melts first; include procedural sequence so others can reproduce.
